projects.title: Web Application Security Assessment Notebook
projects.summary: A structured framework for documenting an authorized web application assessment, from scope definition to evidence, risk analysis, remediation, and retesting.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: A reusable framework for recording the methodology and results of an authorized web application security assessment. Publish as a completed case study only after adding evidence from actual work.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.body: Maintain a repeatable assessment process and communicate technical risk and remediation clearly.

sections.heading: Scope and authorization
sections.body: Record written authorization, in-scope assets, test windows, exclusions, permitted techniques, data-handling rules, and stop conditions before testing.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.body: Document application mapping, identity and access-control checks, session handling, input validation, business logic, and other relevant test areas. Use an established methodology such as the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide where appropriate.

sections.heading: Findings and evidence
sections.body: Add only verified observations. Include sanitized, reproducible evidence and remove secrets, personal data, and sensitive infrastructure details.

sections.heading: Risk and remediation
sections.body: Explain likelihood and impact in context, support severity ratings with evidence, and propose practical remediation.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.body: Record retest results and lessons learned before presenting the assessment as completed.

projects.title: Security Automation Tool
projects.summary: Project space for a security utility, including its problem statement, implementation, tests, limitations, and usage documentation.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Describe the security problem the tool is intended to solve and link to the source repository once it is available.

sections.heading: Design
sections.body: Document the expected inputs and outputs, operating environment, dependencies, and safe operational boundaries.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.body: Provide tests, sample outputs, known limitations, and reproducible steps to verify behavior.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
sections.body: Record implementation decisions and lessons supported by the actual development work.

projects.title: CTF & Ethical Codebreaking Field Notes
projects.summary: A place for documented challenge analysis, hypotheses, evidence, and lessons learned from authorized competitions and labs.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Add a specific challenge or lab name and explain the learning objective.

sections.heading: Rules and publication
sections.body: Follow the competition rules and confirm that publishing a solution is permitted.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.body: Explain the assumptions, hypotheses, tools, evidence, and reasoning behind the approach.

sections.heading: Results and lessons
sections.body: Report only verified results and reflect on the techniques or concepts learned.

articles.title: Before the Tools: Define the Scope
articles.summary: Why clear authorization and test boundaries are essential to a useful security assessment.

sections.heading: Start with permission
sections.body: A security assessment begins with explicit permission and a shared understanding of what may be tested.

sections.heading: Make the boundary concrete
sections.body: Record assets, test windows, permitted techniques, exclusions, data-handling requirements, and stop conditions. Resolve ambiguity with the system owner before testing.

sections.heading: Keep evidence proportionate
sections.body: Collect only the evidence needed to explain and reproduce an observation. Redact credentials, personal information, and sensitive infrastructure details.

sections.heading: Close the loop
sections.body: Connect each verified finding to risk and remediation. Retesting should confirm that the underlying control works, not merely that one test case no longer succeeds.

articles.title: Writing Technical Notes Others Can Reproduce
articles.summary: A practical approach to documenting environments, observations, evidence, and conclusions.

sections.heading: Write for the next reader
sections.body: Explain the environment, assumptions, and purpose of each important step so another researcher can follow the reasoning.

sections.heading: Record the environment
sections.body: Document relevant versions and configuration without exposing secrets or private target data.

sections.heading: Separate evidence from interpretation
sections.body: Describe what was observed before explaining what it may mean. State uncertainty and limitations explicitly.

sections.heading: Use useful references
sections.body: Link to primary documentation and explain the context in which a conclusion applies.
